title: Family says changes needed to prevent in-custody deaths
article: Family members of a man who died from a drug overdose in police custody say simply making the police detention cells safer isn't good enough.
They say more systemic changes are needed to prevent similar deaths in the future.

"The problem is much bigger than what happened in the jail. If these people had homes to go to, they wouldn't be sleeping on the street, they wouldn't get picked up and put in a jail cell," Kelly Murtland said.

Murtland's ex-husband, Doug Morissette, died alone in a police holding cell from a lethal combination of methadone and alcohol. He had been arrested for public intoxication on a downtown street corner less than 12 hours earlier.

A weeklong coroner's inquest into Morissette's death culminated Thursday with eight recommendations from the jury, intended to make police detention safer. The recommendations include having a paramedic on the unit 24 hours a day, improving the level of care for intoxicated people and increasing staff levels in the detention area during busy times.
Murtland said the jury's recommendations don't go far enough.
"You are fighting for his voice and his life. It just seemed (that) ultimately there won't be any change."

Madison Murtland, Morissette's daughter, said she agrees with the jury that the paramedics on shift should pay closer attention to people who are brought in for public intoxication. The jury said the paramedics should keep an accurate log book when they check on prisoners.
Madison said she hopes the recommendations are actually put into practice.
"Whether or not they are implemented or not would be what I'm concerned about," she said.

A previous inquest into the death of Brandon Daniels, who died in police custody in 2010, resulted in recommendations that included increasing paramedic hours and the number of beds at the city's brief detox unit. Nearly a year has passed since that inquest, and those recommendations have not been implemented.
Madison said she agrees with her mother that the jury failed to recommend solutions to the "bigger problems," like why her father ended up in police custody in the first place.
"I would like to see those recommendations put in place so it doesn't happen again, so no one else has to go through what we went through," Madison said.
Kelly Murtland said while the inquest failed to grapple with the larger issues of addictions and homelessness, it did provide closure for her family.
Morissette was 57 at the time of his death and was only weeks away from becoming a grandfather.
